source.title: Explaining How Visual, Textual and Multimodal Encoders Share Concepts
source.authors: Clément Cornet; Romaric Besançon; H. Le Borgne

page_placements.theme: Conditional cross-model feature sharing and alignment

record.tranche_reason: The study applies SAE-based feature analysis to visual, textual, and multimodal encoders and reports results about SAE-derived features in these model settings. It does not test the original toy-network superposition mechanism.
record.gate_note: The paper trains TopK SAEs and reports interpreted feature groups and cross-model correlations. The wMPPC tables compare feature sharing across encoders; they do not measure superposition geometry, feature sparsity or importance tradeoffs, neuron polysemanticity, or whether SAE features are complete or canonical. No results are inferred from cited work.
record.test_reason: The study uses TopK SAEs as a tool to compare 21 visual, textual and multimodal encoders through cross-model feature correlation (wMPPC, Comparative Sharedness). Its results concern cross-model and cross-modal feature sharing. It does not test whether real models contain sparse features an SAE can recover as evidence of superposition. It takes SAE features as concepts by assumption ('each feature representing a distinct semantic concept'). It has no reconstruction, sparsity-versus-dimension or interpretability-rate measure, and no neuron-level polysemanticity measure. The qualitative typology covers only the top 1% of features, chosen by a sharedness score, so it is not a test of recoverability.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that cross-modal shared information lies mostly in the last layer. They also conclude that wMPPC reveals differences in image-text alignment quality between datasets (COCO is better than a Laion subset).
record.recipe_differences: The study uses TopK SAEs and feature-correlation/sharedness measures on pretrained encoders; it does not reproduce the toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported wMPPC varies with layer selection, input dataset, model size, and source/target modality. The feature typologies are based on COCO and selected top comparative-sharedness features.

fits_no_version.finding: Cross-model wMPPC between SAE features: same-modality similarity is higher than cross-modal similarity. Cross-modal sharing concentrates in the last layer. Cross-modal wMPPC is lower on Laion and Flowers than on COCO. Results are similar at B and L sizes (Tables 1–3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE-feature similarity across encoders depends on modality, layer, dataset and model size.

fits_no_version.finding: Two SAEs trained with different seeds on the same CLIP-ViT-B/32 encoder reach wMPPC 0.585 (shuffled control 0.0125). This is reported only to validate the metric, not as a stability test.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features trained with different seeds on the same model are only partly matched by maximum correlation.

record.problems: The study itself states that SAEs are not guaranteed to extract every concept. The reported feature interpretations are qualitative and selected from the highest comparative-sharedness features; the study does not establish feature completeness or causal relevance.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many separate wMPPC tables across individual encoders and conditions. These are not included as claim-version rows because they measure cross-model SAE-feature similarity rather than superposition, neuron polysemanticity, or direct feature recoverability. The aggregate patterns are summarized under fits_no_version.

untested.parts: No toy models, no sparsity sweep, no geometry.
No neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity analysis.
No alternative causes of polysemanticity examined.
SAEs are applied, but recoverability, reconstruction quality, the share of interpretable features and distributed neuron coding are not measured. SAE features are assumed to be concepts.
Completeness, stability and canonical status are not tested. Two-seed SAE wMPPC (0.585) is reported only as a metric control. The authors note SAEs may not extract every concept.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' with a V4 'supports' label overreads the paper. It presupposes SAE features as interpretable concepts and builds comparison metrics on top of them. The cited Toy Models paper appears only in related work as motivation.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-over-dimension sweep, sparsity transition, or regular superposition geometry.
No test of neuron polysemanticity as capacity competition or of dedicated dimensions for important features.
No test of alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity indicates superposition.

The study analyzes encoder models, including BERT and DeBERTa, rather than generative LLMs generally. It does not measure feature spread across neurons, nor independently validate SAE feature completeness or causal use by the encoders.
No systematic test of SAE feature completeness, stability, or canonical status. The authors note as a limitation that SAEs are not guaranteed to extract every concept.
No test of whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional subspaces.

rows.subject: CLIP ViT L/14 (image encoder)
rows.operation_detail: Trained a TopK SAE on encoder activations and inspected the top 1% of comparative sharedness features against other VLM visual encoders and visual foundation models.

conditions.value: SigLIP2 and DFN visual encoders plus a different-seed CLIP SAE versus DinoV2, MambaVision, and ViT

rows.measure: Qualitative categories among SAE features with high comparative sharedness
rows.value: Reported categories include age-related situations, pets with unusual behaviour, rooms of the house, vehicles, old photos, geographical concepts, and a feature associated with “to ride”; the authors report that these were better shared with the VLM group than with the visual foundation models.
rows.note: The paper interprets selected SAE features as semantic concepts; this supports recovery of interpretable SAE features in an encoder setting, not feature completeness or causal validity.
rows.check: This is a selected set: the top 1% of features by Generalized Comparative Sharedness, interpreted qualitatively. It measures which CLIP visual SAE features are shared with VLMs rather than visual FMs, not whether the model contains recoverable sparse features. It does not bear on V4 and cannot show V4's effect.

rows.subject: CLIP ViT L/14 (image encoder)
rows.operation_detail: Inspected comparative sharedness of the image encoder's SAE features with text encoders versus visual foundation models.

conditions.value: BERT-large and DeBERTa-large versus MambaVision, DinoV2, and ViT

rows.measure: Qualitative categories and overlap among high comparative-sharedness SAE features
rows.value: Reported categories include kids in specific situations, rooms of the house, types of vehicles, pets with unusual behaviour, and old photos; 16 features were among the highest 81 for both the LLM and VLM comparisons.
rows.note: These are features from a visual encoder compared with text encoders, not a direct analysis of SAE features extracted from BERT or DeBERTa.
rows.check: This is a selected top-1% sharedness set comparing CLIP image SAE features with BERT/DeBERTa SAE features. It measures cross-modal sharing, not superposition or SAE recoverability. Same problem as r1.

rows.subject: CLIP ViT B/32 (visual encoder)
rows.operation_detail: Compared wMPPC for two SAEs on the same encoder with and without shuffling features across images.
rows.note: The shuffle control is used to assess the correlation measure, not superposition or feature recoverability directly.
rows.check: This is a significance control for the wMPPC metric (shuffled 0.0125 vs 0.5854), not a result on any version. 'Absent' is not meaningful against a version.

source_check.correct: CLIP ViT B/32 visual encoder: 87M parameters, pretrained. Non-shuffled wMPPC = 0.5854; shuffled wMPPC = 0.0125.

relation.reason: SAEs provide the comparison tool; the shuffle control assesses wMPPC significance rather than superposition, feature recoverability, or canonical SAE units.

tranche.reason: Uses SAE-derived features to study cross-model concept sharing and validate its correlation indicator; does not test a superposition claim version.

source_check.notes: The shuffle control supports metric validation only. The discussion's caveat about incomplete concept extraction is not an empirical test of SAE completeness.

statements.correction: Appendix B: two SAEs trained on the same CLIP-ViT-B/32 visual encoder using COCO; non-shuffled wMPPC = 0.5854 (0.585 rounded); shuffled wMPPC = 0.0125; training seeds unspecified.
statements.problem: The values and metric-validation interpretation are correct, but Appendix B does not specify different training seeds for this pair of SAEs.
